screens.title: Why Prometheus and Grafana?
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we introduce two complementary open-source projects that drive modern monitoring: Prometheus and Grafana. You'll learn what each project is built to do, how their design choices make them well suited for cloud-native and Kubernetes environments, and why engineers often pair them to get robust data collection plus powerful visualization. Prometheus focuses on metrics: it uses a multi-dimensional data model where every measurement has a name and labeled dimensions, and it gathers data primarily by scraping targets on a schedule. Grafana is the visualization layer: it connects to data stores like Prometheus and transforms raw time-series into dashboards that help you spot trends and investigate incidents. We will also preview the ecosystem pieces you will meet later, like exporters that expose metrics from systems, a Pushgateway for short-lived jobs that need to push metrics, and Alertmanager which groups and routes alerts. By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain each tool’s primary role and see a simple real-world scenario, such as monitoring a Kubernetes cluster, where Prometheus supplies the metrics and Grafana organizes them into actionable dashboards. Consider how a pull model simplifies discovery in dynamic environments and why labels matter for flexible querying.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to the skills you'll practice. First, you'll explain Prometheus's core purpose and design philosophy as a monitoring system: that it stores time-series metrics in a multi-dimensional model identified by names and labels and collects data primarily by scraping targets. Understanding this helps you choose Prometheus for dynamic environments where services scale or change often. Second, you'll describe Grafana's role as a visualization and dashboarding platform. Grafana isn't a data store; it connects to sources like Prometheus, Loki, or databases and transforms raw metrics into dashboards and alerts. By learning these two roles you will be able to recommend the right tool for collection versus visualization, and avoid common role confusion. Each objective includes a short example to anchor the idea: for Prometheus, imagine a metric with labels for method and path; for Grafana, think of a dashboard that switches its scope using a template variable. These skills matter because clear role assignment prevents building brittle monitoring systems and helps maintain reliable incident workflows.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Continuing the objectives, you'll also learn to name typical use cases and strengths of the Prometheus plus Grafana solution. For instance, Prometheus is well suited to real-time monitoring of service metrics in environments where services start and stop frequently, because its pull-based scraper integrates with service discovery. Grafana is well suited for building dashboards that combine data from Prometheus and other sources, enabling consolidated troubleshooting views. You will also learn to spot common pitfalls, such as relying on Prometheus for long-term log storage, which is not what it is optimized for, or misconfiguring Alertmanager so that alerts flood your team. These objectives will prepare you to build a simple monitoring workflow: instrument an application, run an exporter if needed, let Prometheus scrape the metrics, route alerts through Alertmanager, and visualize the result in Grafana. Practice scenarios will help you map each component to its responsibility and avoid role confusion during architecture decisions.

screens.title: Prometheus: purpose and data model
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus is a monitoring system and a time-series database built around a multi-dimensional metric model. That means every metric is defined by a metric name and a set of label key-value pairs that together identify a single time series. For example, a metric name might represent total HTTP requests, and labels can include method, path, and status. This design lets you slice and group measurements in many ways without changing instrumentation. The pull-based scrape model is another core idea: Prometheus discovers targets and periodically scrapes metrics from them, which simplifies monitoring workloads that scale or move because you rely on service discovery rather than manually registering each instance. Prometheus stores scraped data on a local time-series database optimized for metrics. A common misconception is to treat Prometheus like a log store for long-term retention; it is optimized for metrics and short-to-medium term retention. Practically, you will encounter exporters that translate existing systems into Prometheus metrics, a Pushgateway for ephemeral jobs that cannot be scraped, and Alertmanager which processes alerts triggered from Prometheus queries. Think of Prometheus as the engine that collects, stores, and answers time-series questions about your system.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Prometheus stores labeled time-series metrics and scrapes targets on a schedule, making it fit for dynamic, cloud-native infrastructures.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Prometheus: data model
Definition

Multi-dimensional metrics

A metric is a name plus labels. Labels let you tag measurements with dimensions like method, path, or status so queries can aggregate flexibly.

Metric example
http_requests_total{method="POST", path="/api/users", status="200"}
Why labels matter
Labels let you aggregate, filter, and compare by dimensions without changing application instrumentation when new query needs arise.
Common misconception
Prometheus is not a long-term log store. High-cardinality events and raw logs require different storage than a metrics TSDB.
Supporting concepts
Scrape model
Prometheus discovers targets and pulls metrics, which eases monitoring dynamic services.
Local TSDB
Scraped samples are stored locally in an append-optimized time-series database designed for metrics.
Ecosystem pieces
Exporters expose existing systems, Pushgateway handles pushed metrics for ephemeral jobs, and Alertmanager routes alerts.
Key Takeaway

Prometheus's label-driven model and pull-based scraping make it flexible for modern, dynamic infrastructures.

screens.title: Pull model and service discovery
screens.narratorSegment: The pull model is a defining operational choice for Prometheus. Instead of having every application push its metrics to a central collector, Prometheus discovers targets and periodically scrapes an HTTP endpoint each target exposes. This approach simplifies discovery in environments where instances appear and disappear frequently, because Prometheus integrates with service discovery mechanisms to keep its target list current. A typical flow starts with service discovery learning active endpoints, followed by the scraper performing an HTTP scrape on each target, ingesting labeled samples into the TSDB, and finally exposing an A P I for queries and alert evaluation. Exporters are often the scrape targets for systems that do not natively export Prometheus metrics. A misconception is thinking the pull model prevents short-lived jobs from being monitored; this is why a Pushgateway exists to accept pushed metrics from ephemeral tasks and make them available for Prometheus to scrape indirectly. Understanding this flow helps you design monitoring for orchestration platforms like Kubernetes where automatic discovery is essential. Pull model and service discovery means prometheus discovers targets, scrapes metrics over http, stores samples in tsdb, and uses labels to index time-series for queries.. In practical terms, how prometheus finds and scrapes targets in dynamic environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Prometheus discovers targets, scrapes metrics over HTTP, stores samples in TSDB, and uses labels to index time-series for queries.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Pull model & discovery
Process Flow

Discovery → Scrape → Store → Query

1. Service discovery
Prometheus learns active targets from sources like orchestration APIs or DNS.
2. Scrape
Prometheus periodically requests metrics endpoints and ingests returned samples.
3. Store
Samples are appended to Prometheus's TSDB for time-based queries.
Example scenario
In Kubernetes, Prometheus can discover pods matching a label selector and automatically scrape each pod's metrics endpoint as containers scale up and down.
Edge case
For very short-lived batch jobs, Pushgateway offers a safe alternative by allowing metrics to be pushed and then scraped later by Prometheus.
Pro tip
Use service discovery integrations to avoid manual target lists — this keeps monitoring resilient as your environment changes.
Check your understanding
Why does a pull model simplify monitoring in environments with frequent scaling events? What gap does a Pushgateway fill?
Key Takeaway

Prometheus's pull-based scraping paired with service discovery reduces manual configuration and adapts to dynamic topologies.

screens.title: Exporters, Pushgateway, and Alertmanager
screens.narratorSegment: The Prometheus ecosystem extends the core server with components that fill integration and operational gaps. Exporters are adapters that expose metrics from systems that do not natively speak Prometheus metrics. Common examples include host-level exporters for operating system metrics and Kubernetes exporters that expose cluster object states. Exporters make it easy to monitor third-party systems without changing their internals. The Pushgateway is a small, focused component for scenarios where a pull model is impractical — typically ephemeral or batch jobs that do their work and exit before a scrape can occur. Jobs can push their metrics to the Pushgateway, and Prometheus then scrapes the Pushgateway so those metrics appear in time series. Alertmanager receives alerts from Prometheus evaluation, deduplicates and groups them, and routes notifications to receivers such as email or pager systems. A common operational pitfall is not configuring Alertmanager routing rules carefully, which can cause alert storms. Knowing each component’s role helps you design monitoring that is reliable and maintainable. Exporters, Pushgateway, and Alertmanager means exporters adapt systems to prometheus; pushgateway handles ephemeral job metrics; alertmanager manages alerts and notifications.. In practical terms, roles in the prometheus ecosystem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Exporters adapt systems to Prometheus; Pushgateway handles ephemeral job metrics; Alertmanager manages alerts and notifications.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Exporters & components
Definition

Key ecosystem components

Exporters
Adapters that expose metrics from systems like databases, hosts, or orchestration components in Prometheus format. Example: a node exporter for host metrics.
Pushgateway
Accepts pushed metrics from short-lived processes, so Prometheus can scrape them later. Use it for ephemeral jobs that cannot be scraped directly.
Alertmanager
Receives alerts from Prometheus, groups and deduplicates them, and routes notifications to receivers. Proper configuration avoids alert storms and noisy notifications.
Scenario
A nightly batch job pushes summary metrics to Pushgateway so its success rate is visible in Prometheus even after the job exits.
Misconfiguration risk
If Alertmanager routing is too broad, unrelated alerts may group together and cause confusion; design routes by team and severity.
Concrete example
Use a node exporter to expose CPU and memory metrics from hosts, kube-state-metrics to expose Kubernetes object health, and configure Alertmanager to route critical alerts to on-call channels while sending low-priority issues to a team inbox.
Key Takeaway

Use exporters to adapt systems, Pushgateway for ephemeral jobs, and Alertmanager to control how alerts reach responders.

screens.title: PromQL: what it enables
screens.narratorSegment: PromQL is the query language Prometheus provides for selecting and aggregating time-series data. It is designed to let you express selections over metric names and label sets, and to perform real-time aggregations and calculations on those series. With PromQL you can compute rates, group by labels, and build expressions that feed both dashboards and alerting rules. This makes Prometheus very effective for identifying trends and troubleshooting: instead of scanning raw numeric dumps, you write queries that summarize behavior over time. A practical example from the metric model is a total HTTP requests metric annotated with method, path, and status labels; PromQL enables you to filter that metric for a specific path and compute requests per second or error ratios. A common misconception is trying to use PromQL as a replacement for complex log analysis; PromQL is built for numeric time-series and is best paired with log stores when you need high-cardinality event data. Learning the basics of PromQL will let you define precise alerting rules and craft dashboard panels that highlight the most important signals. PromQL: what it enables means a functional query language that selects and aggregates labeled time-series to support dashboarding and alerting.. In practical terms, a powerful query language for time-series analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PromQL
keyIdea.text: A functional query language that selects and aggregates labeled time-series to support dashboarding and alerting.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › PromQL overview
Definition

Querying labeled time-series

PromQL helps you filter by metric name and labels, aggregate by dimensions, and compute derived values that drive dashboards and alerts.

Metric identity reminder
Remember the metric example with labels: http_requests_total with method, path, and status labels. PromQL uses that same identity to select matching series.
Where you use it
PromQL is used in dashboard panels and alerting rules so queries produce the numeric signals you visualize and act upon.
Concrete guidance
Example use
Filter a metric by path and compute rate over a time window to detect rising request rates for a particular endpoint.
Misconception
PromQL is not a log query language. Use it for numeric time-series; pair it with a log store when you need raw event details.
Practice tip
Start by identifying the metric name and labels you need, then write a focused selection before adding aggregations or transformations.
Key Takeaway

PromQL converts labeled metrics into meaningful signals for dashboards and alerts, but it is focused on numeric time-series rather than raw logs.

screens.title: Grafana: dashboards and data sources
screens.narratorSegment: Grafana provides a universal visualization and exploration layer that can connect to many backends. Its core strength is dashboarding: building panels with graphs, tables, heatmaps, and gauges that make operational signals obvious. Importantly, Grafana is data source agnostic. It queries data where it lives, whether that is Prometheus for metrics, a log store for events, or a database for business data. That separation means Grafana itself does not replace a metrics store; instead it federates queries, combines different signals, and displays them in unified dashboards. Grafana also supports templating: variables that let a single dashboard adapt to different services, namespaces, or instances so you can reuse panels across environments. Grafana can define alerts directly on panels for simple thresholds, but teams often keep complex routing in Alertmanager for Prometheus-originated alerts. A practical takeaway is to treat Grafana as the place you go to explore and correlate signals during incidents, not as the primary data collector or long-term store. Grafana: dashboards and data sources means grafana queries and visualizes data from external sources, enabling dashboard-driven investigation and correlation.. In practical terms, grafana as a visualization layer, not a storage engine. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Grafana queries and visualizes data from external sources, enabling dashboard-driven investigation and correlation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Grafana overview
Architecture

Visualization and data federation

Grafana connects to many data sources, queries them at panel time, and displays unified dashboards for analysis and incident response.

Dashboarding
Create panels for metrics and combine them to tell a system health story. Interactive features like time range selection help exploration.
Data source agnostic
Grafana queries Prometheus or other backends; it does not act as the primary storage for those sources.
Practical items
Templating
Use variables so dashboards can switch context between services or clusters without duplicating panels.
Alerting note
Grafana supports basic alerting on panels, but teams commonly rely on Alertmanager for complex routing and deduplication of alerts raised by Prometheus.
Key Takeaway

Treat Grafana as the visualization and exploration layer that queries your data where it lives and helps teams act on insights.

screens.title: Prometheus vs Grafana — roles compared
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the separation of responsibilities between Prometheus and Grafana is critical to designing reliable monitoring. Prometheus is responsible for collecting metrics, storing them in a time-series database, and answering queries via PromQL. Grafana is responsible for querying data from external sources and presenting that data as dashboards and visualizations. A simple way to remember this difference is: Prometheus is the data engine, Grafana is the visualization console. Practically, an engineer uses Prometheus to scrape application and infrastructure metrics, write PromQL expressions for alerts, and persist samples. The same engineer uses Grafana to assemble panels, add templates to switch contexts, and to combine signals from Prometheus and other systems into a single dashboard. A common mistake is trying to use Grafana as a long-term store or to rely on Grafana panel alerts for complex cross-source routing; instead, keep Prometheus for metric queries and Alertmanager for routing complex alert workflows. When you pair the two correctly, workflows for troubleshooting and on-call response become far more efficient. Prometheus vs Grafana — roles compared means prometheus = collect, store, query. grafana = query external stores, visualize, and explore.. In practical terms, which tool handles collection, storage, querying, and display. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Inspecting a metric example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's inspect a concrete metric example to make labels and identity tangible. Consider a metric that records total HTTP requests annotated with labels for method, path, and status. The metric name identifies what is being measured; the labels describe dimensions such as which HTTP method or endpoint the request used. Reading labels aloud helps avoid confusion: say the metric records HTTP requests for the POST method to the users A P I returning status two hundred. screens.title: Common pitfalls and operational guidance
screens.narratorSegment: When you adopt Prometheus and Grafana, several operational pitfalls commonly occur. First, alert storms: if Alertmanager routing is not carefully configured, many alerts may reach the same receiver at once, overwhelming responders. Group alerts by team and severity, and tune alert thresholds so they reflect actionable conditions. Second, high-cardinality labels: adding labels with very many unique values, such as user IDs or request identifiers, can dramatically increase the number of series Prometheus stores and hurt performance. Only label dimensions you will aggregate or group by. Third, role confusion: do not expect Grafana to be a metrics store; it queries other backends. Keep Prometheus for metric collection and querying, and use Grafana for visual correlation. Also be cautious about retention expectations — Prometheus is optimized for metric storage but may not be the best place for decades-long retention of raw samples. Finally, instrument thoughtfully: choose sensible metric names and labels so that PromQL queries and Grafana panels remain understandable and maintainable. Awareness of these challenges will help you build a resilient monitoring setup. Common pitfalls and operational guidance means tune alerts, limit label cardinality, and keep responsibilities clear between data collection and visualization to maintain a healthy monitoring stack.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we introduce two complementary open-source projects that drive modern monitoring: Prometheus and Grafana. You'll learn what each project is built to do, how their design choices make them well suited for cloud-native and Kubernetes environments, and why engineers often pair them to get robust data collection plus powerful visualization. Prometheus focuses on metrics: it uses a multi-dimensional data model where every measurement has a name and labeled dimensions, and it gathers data primarily by scraping targets on a schedule. Grafana is the visualization layer: it connects to data stores like Prometheus and transforms raw time-series into dashboards that help you spot trends and investigate incidents. We will also preview the ecosystem pieces you will meet later, like exporters that expose metrics from systems, a Pushgateway for short-lived jobs that need to push metrics, and Alertmanager which groups and routes alerts. By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain each tool’s primary role and see a simple real-world scenario, such as monitoring a Kubernetes cluster, where Prometheus supplies the metrics and Grafana organizes them into actionable dashboards. Consider how a pull model simplifies discovery in dynamic environments and why labels matter for flexible querying.

These objectives map directly to the skills you'll practice. First, you'll explain Prometheus's core purpose and design philosophy as a monitoring system: that it stores time-series metrics in a multi-dimensional model identified by names and labels and collects data primarily by scraping targets. Understanding this helps you choose Prometheus for dynamic environments where services scale or change often. Second, you'll describe Grafana's role as a visualization and dashboarding platform. Grafana isn't a data store; it connects to sources like Prometheus, Loki, or databases and transforms raw metrics into dashboards and alerts. By learning these two roles you will be able to recommend the right tool for collection versus visualization, and avoid common role confusion. Each objective includes a short example to anchor the idea: for Prometheus, imagine a metric with labels for method and path; for Grafana, think of a dashboard that switches its scope using a template variable. These skills matter because clear role assignment prevents building brittle monitoring systems and helps maintain reliable incident workflows.

Continuing the objectives, you'll also learn to name typical use cases and strengths of the Prometheus plus Grafana solution. For instance, Prometheus is well suited to real-time monitoring of service metrics in environments where services start and stop frequently, because its pull-based scraper integrates with service discovery. Grafana is well suited for building dashboards that combine data from Prometheus and other sources, enabling consolidated troubleshooting views. You will also learn to spot common pitfalls, such as relying on Prometheus for long-term log storage, which is not what it is optimized for, or misconfiguring Alertmanager so that alerts flood your team. These objectives will prepare you to build a simple monitoring workflow: instrument an application, run an exporter if needed, let Prometheus scrape the metrics, route alerts through Alertmanager, and visualize the result in Grafana. Practice scenarios will help you map each component to its responsibility and avoid role confusion during architecture decisions.

Prometheus is a monitoring system and a time-series database built around a multi-dimensional metric model. That means every metric is defined by a metric name and a set of label key-value pairs that together identify a single time series. For example, a metric name might represent total HTTP requests, and labels can include method, path, and status. This design lets you slice and group measurements in many ways without changing instrumentation. The pull-based scrape model is another core idea: Prometheus discovers targets and periodically scrapes metrics from them, which simplifies monitoring workloads that scale or move because you rely on service discovery rather than manually registering each instance. Prometheus stores scraped data on a local time-series database optimized for metrics. A common misconception is to treat Prometheus like a log store for long-term retention; it is optimized for metrics and short-to-medium term retention. Practically, you will encounter exporters that translate existing systems into Prometheus metrics, a Pushgateway for ephemeral jobs that cannot be scraped, and Alertmanager which processes alerts triggered from Prometheus queries. Think of Prometheus as the engine that collects, stores, and answers time-series questions about your system.

The pull model is a defining operational choice for Prometheus. Instead of having every application push its metrics to a central collector, Prometheus discovers targets and periodically scrapes an HTTP endpoint each target exposes. This approach simplifies discovery in environments where instances appear and disappear frequently, because Prometheus integrates with service discovery mechanisms to keep its target list current. A typical flow starts with service discovery learning active endpoints, followed by the scraper performing an HTTP scrape on each target, ingesting labeled samples into the TSDB, and finally exposing an A P I for queries and alert evaluation. Exporters are often the scrape targets for systems that do not natively export Prometheus metrics. A misconception is thinking the pull model prevents short-lived jobs from being monitored; this is why a Pushgateway exists to accept pushed metrics from ephemeral tasks and make them available for Prometheus to scrape indirectly. Understanding this flow helps you design monitoring for orchestration platforms like Kubernetes where automatic discovery is essential. Pull model and service discovery means prometheus discovers targets, scrapes metrics over http, stores samples in tsdb, and uses labels to index time-series for queries.. In practical terms, how prometheus finds and scrapes targets in dynamic environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Prometheus ecosystem extends the core server with components that fill integration and operational gaps. Exporters are adapters that expose metrics from systems that do not natively speak Prometheus metrics. Common examples include host-level exporters for operating system metrics and Kubernetes exporters that expose cluster object states. Exporters make it easy to monitor third-party systems without changing their internals. The Pushgateway is a small, focused component for scenarios where a pull model is impractical — typically ephemeral or batch jobs that do their work and exit before a scrape can occur. Jobs can push their metrics to the Pushgateway, and Prometheus then scrapes the Pushgateway so those metrics appear in time series. Alertmanager receives alerts from Prometheus evaluation, deduplicates and groups them, and routes notifications to receivers such as email or pager systems. A common operational pitfall is not configuring Alertmanager routing rules carefully, which can cause alert storms. Knowing each component’s role helps you design monitoring that is reliable and maintainable. Exporters, Pushgateway, and Alertmanager means exporters adapt systems to prometheus; pushgateway handles ephemeral job metrics; alertmanager manages alerts and notifications.. In practical terms, roles in the prometheus ecosystem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

PromQL is the query language Prometheus provides for selecting and aggregating time-series data. It is designed to let you express selections over metric names and label sets, and to perform real-time aggregations and calculations on those series. With PromQL you can compute rates, group by labels, and build expressions that feed both dashboards and alerting rules. This makes Prometheus very effective for identifying trends and troubleshooting: instead of scanning raw numeric dumps, you write queries that summarize behavior over time. A practical example from the metric model is a total HTTP requests metric annotated with method, path, and status labels; PromQL enables you to filter that metric for a specific path and compute requests per second or error ratios. A common misconception is trying to use PromQL as a replacement for complex log analysis; PromQL is built for numeric time-series and is best paired with log stores when you need high-cardinality event data. Learning the basics of PromQL will let you define precise alerting rules and craft dashboard panels that highlight the most important signals. PromQL: what it enables means a functional query language that selects and aggregates labeled time-series to support dashboarding and alerting.. In practical terms, a powerful query language for time-series analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Grafana provides a universal visualization and exploration layer that can connect to many backends. Its core strength is dashboarding: building panels with graphs, tables, heatmaps, and gauges that make operational signals obvious. Importantly, Grafana is data source agnostic. It queries data where it lives, whether that is Prometheus for metrics, a log store for events, or a database for business data. That separation means Grafana itself does not replace a metrics store; instead it federates queries, combines different signals, and displays them in unified dashboards. Grafana also supports templating: variables that let a single dashboard adapt to different services, namespaces, or instances so you can reuse panels across environments. Grafana can define alerts directly on panels for simple thresholds, but teams often keep complex routing in Alertmanager for Prometheus-originated alerts. Understanding the separation of responsibilities between Prometheus and Grafana is critical to designing reliable monitoring. Prometheus is responsible for collecting metrics, storing them in a time-series database, and answering queries via PromQL. Grafana is responsible for querying data from external sources and presenting that data as dashboards and visualizations. A simple way to remember this difference is: Prometheus is the data engine, Grafana is the visualization console. Practically, an engineer uses Prometheus to scrape application and infrastructure metrics, write PromQL expressions for alerts, and persist samples. The same engineer uses Grafana to assemble panels, add templates to switch contexts, and to combine signals from Prometheus and other systems into a single dashboard. A common mistake is trying to use Grafana as a long-term store or to rely on Grafana panel alerts for complex cross-source routing; instead, keep Prometheus for metric queries and Alertmanager for routing complex alert workflows. When you pair the two correctly, workflows for troubleshooting and on-call response become far more efficient. When you adopt Prometheus and Grafana, several operational pitfalls commonly occur. First, alert storms: if Alertmanager routing is not carefully configured, many alerts may reach the same receiver at once, overwhelming responders. Group alerts by team and severity, and tune alert thresholds so they reflect actionable conditions. Second, high-cardinality labels: adding labels with very many unique values, such as user IDs or request identifiers, can dramatically increase the number of series Prometheus stores and hurt performance. Only label dimensions you will aggregate or group by. Third, role confusion: do not expect Grafana to be a metrics store; it queries other backends. Keep Prometheus for metric collection and querying, and use Grafana for visual correlation. Also be cautious about retention expectations — Prometheus is optimized for metric storage but may not be the best place for decades-long retention of raw samples. Finally, instrument thoughtfully: choose sensible metric names and labels so that PromQL queries and Grafana panels remain understandable and maintainable. Awareness of these challenges will help you build a resilient monitoring setup. These are the core concepts to hold onto. Prometheus is a metrics collection and time-series storage system built around a multi-dimensional model of metric names and labels. It scrapes targets using a pull model which works well with service discovery in dynamic infrastructures. Grafana is the visualization and dashboarding layer that connects to Prometheus and many other data sources; it is not a storage engine. PromQL is the language Prometheus provides to select and aggregate labeled time-series for dashboards and alerts. Exporters, Pushgateway, and Alertmanager are ecosystem pieces that adapt third-party systems, support ephemeral jobs, and manage alert delivery respectively. Keep these roles clear: Prometheus collects and answers metric queries; Grafana visualizes and correlates them. This separation enables a flexible, maintainable monitoring stack that supports detection, investigation, and action.
